Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e103.summary: Rubric-like opening paragraph transcribing the running head for the distinction: it names Distinction 54 of Book II and states its topic, 'De potestate peccandi, et obedientia' (on the power to sin, and obedience). It functions as a section label rather than as argument.

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e119.summary: Opens the divisio textus (lectio-style accessus) for the final distinction of Book II, glossing the Master's opening words ('Post praedicta consideratione dignum'). It states that in this 44th (i.e. final) distinction Peter Lombard raises the question whether the power/potency to sin belongs to us from God, from the devil, or from ourselves, and announces that the Master's text divides into three parts, the first of which is the part 'quod dictum est' now being treated.
claims: Lombard's distinction 54 raises the question of the origin of the power to sin (from God, the devil, or man himself)
The Master's text in this distinction divides into three parts

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e143.summary: Identifies the second of the three main parts of the Master's text: because the preceding part had spoken of 'power,' and power entails an obligation to obey it, the Master here raises the question of obedience itself.
claims: The second part of the distinction's text raises the question of obedience, following from the prior discussion of power

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e152.summary: Identifies the third of the three main parts of the Master's text: the transition (continuatio) by which the Master links this distinction to the following book of the Sentences.
claims: The third part of the distinction's text is a transitional continuation linking Book II to the next book

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e160.summary: Locates the second and third of the three main parts by their incipits in the Master's text ('Hic oritur quaestio' and 'Iam nunc his intelligendis'), then begins subdividing the first part into three further sections, the first of which raises the question whether the power to sin has its being from God.
claims: The first main part further divides into three subsections
The first subsection raises the question whether the power to sin derives its being from God

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e171.summary: Identifies the second subsection of the first part: it narrates an opinion held by certain unnamed authors who maintain that the power (or potency) to sin is not from God, just as the will to sin is not from God.
claims: An opinion reported (not endorsed) in the text: the power/potency to sin is not from God, analogous to the will to sin not being from God

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e182.summary: Identifies the third subsection of the first part: the Master determines the truth of the question by authority, showing that no power whatsoever exists except from God -- neither the power to sin, to act badly, to harm others, nor to rule and govern others. This resolves and rejects the opinion reported in the preceding paragraph.
claims: All power -- to sin, to harm, or to govern -- comes from God alone, established by authority (auctoritas)

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e195.summary: Locates the second and third subsections just treated by their incipits ('Putant quidem &c.' and 'sed pluribus sanctorum'), then turns to the second main part of the distinction (at 'Hic oritur quaestio'), where the Master raises the question of obedience: given that all power to sin, harm, or govern is from God alone, whether power must always be obeyed and never resisted. States this second part itself has two subsections, the first of which simply raises the question.
claims: Given that power is from God alone, the question arises whether power must always be obeyed and never resisted

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e215.summary: Identifies the second subsection of the obedience part: the Master's solution to the question of obedience (located at incipit 'sed sciendum'). Then turns to the third main part of the distinction (the continuation to the following book, i.e. Book III), noting it likewise divides into two, the first of which recapitulates what has been said.
claims: The Master provides a solution to the question of obedience
The transition to Book III itself divides into two subsections

Gi9qrR-m201200-d1e228.summary: Identifies the second subsection of the transition to Book III: the Master determines the order and subject matter of all four books of the Sentences, specifying what has been treated in Books I and II and what remains to be treated in Books III and IV. The paragraph, and with it the divisio, closes by noting that this concludes the sense of the present lectio, of the distinction, and of the whole of Book II.
claims: The Sentences' four books have a determinate order and division of subject matter, with Books I-II completed and III-IV still to come

Gi9qrR-m201200.summary: Giles of Rome's divisio textus (accessus-style lectio preamble) to Distinction 54, the final distinction of Book II of Peter Lombard's Sentences, on the topic 'De potestate peccandi, et obedientia.' The commentary does not argue a disputed question in utrumque-partes form but methodically segments the Master's text into three main parts -- (1) the question of whether the power to sin is from God, the devil, or man, resolved by authority in favor of all power deriving from God alone; (2) the consequent question of obedience, namely whether power so derived must always be obeyed; and (3) the transitional continuation to Book III, which culminates in an overview of the order and subject matter of all four books of the Sentences. Each part is further subdivided and located by textual incipit, in the standard scholastic lectio manner.
